chunks: Duty cycle from a Vout/Vin ratio. The question: Given a Vout/Vin ratio, how can the duty cycle be calculated?
For a buck in continuous conduction, the duty cycle equals the output voltage divided by the input voltage. So if you are given the ratio, you already have D . The ratio 0.
275 means the switch is on 27. 5 percent of each cycle.
Picture a clock face for one cycle. The switch is on for a slice of the clock and off for the rest. A ratio of 0. 25 means a quarter slice, and 0. 5 means half.
The ratio is simply the size of the slice. The slice picture assumes the converter never runs out of current at light load.
On-time is a straight line in M , with slope 1 over f sw . Below the red line (100 nanoseconds, illustrative) the converter can't produce the pulse.
At 2 megahertz every ratio under 0. 2 is below that line, while at 500 kilohertz the limit is M equals 0. 05 .
Voltage ratio: V out over V in . Duty cycle ( D ): the fraction of the period the switch is on ("What is duty cycle"). Period ( T ): the time of one full cycle, 1 over f .
On-time: D times T , the real time the switch stays on. Continuous conduction (CCM): the inductor current never falls to zero ("What sets a buck's output voltage").
The ratio is 3. 3 over 12 equals 0. 275 , so D equals 27. 5 percent. At 500 kilohertz the period is 2 microseconds, so the on-time is 550 nanoseconds.
A deeper step, 12 volts to 1 volts, gives D about 0. 083 and an on-time of about 170 nanoseconds, which some controllers cannot produce. That is the whole idea.
